F1.quote: Introducing the first model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions, designed to help historians better interpret, attribute and restore fragmentary texts.
F1.claim: the operator's definition: the first model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions, to help historians interpret, attribute and restore fragmentary texts
F1.lineage: what it is: a model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions

F2.quote: Today, we’re publishing a paper in Nature introducing Aeneas , the first artificial intelligence (AI) model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions.
F2.claim: introduced in a Nature paper on the post's date as the first AI model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions
F2.lineage: what it is: a model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions

F3.quote: historians traditionally rely on their expertise and specialized resources to identify “parallels” — which are texts that share similarities in wording, syntax, standardized formulas or provenance.
F3.claim: parallels defined: texts sharing wording, syntax, standardized formulas or provenance, found by historians through expertise and specialized resources
F3.lineage: parallels: what they are and how the model retrieves them

F4.quote: It reasons across thousands of Latin inscriptions, retrieving textual and contextual parallels in seconds that allow historians to interpret and build upon the model’s findings.
F4.claim: the model retrieves textual and contextual parallels across thousands of Latin inscriptions in seconds, for historians to interpret and build on
F4.lineage: parallels: what they are and how the model retrieves them

F5.quote: Our model can also be adapted to other ancient languages, scripts and media, from papyri to coinage, expanding its capabilities to help draw connections across a wider range of historical evidence.
F5.claim: the model is stated to be adaptable to other ancient languages, scripts and media, from papyri to coinage
F5.lineage: the stated reach: other languages, scripts and media

F6.quote: We co-developed Aeneas with the University of Nottingham, and in partnership with researchers at the Universities of Warwick, Oxford and Athens University of Economics and Business (AUEB).
F6.claim: co-developed with the University of Nottingham, with researchers at Warwick, Oxford and AUEB
F6.lineage: who made it: DeepMind, the partners, the authors

F7.quote: we’re making an interactive version of Aeneas freely-available to researchers, students, educators, museum professionals and more at predictingthepast.com . To support further research, we’re also open-sourcing our code and dataset .
F7.claim: an interactive version is free at predictingthepast.com; code and dataset are open-sourced
F7.lineage: access: the interface, the code, the dataset, the licence

F8.quote: Named after the wandering hero of Graeco-Roman mythology, Aeneas builds upon Ithaca , our earlier work using AI to restore, date and place ancient Greek inscriptions.
F8.claim: named after the wandering hero; builds upon Ithaca, DeepMind's earlier model for ancient Greek inscriptions
F8.lineage: lineage and name: Ithaca, the hero

F9.quote: Parallels search: It searches for parallels across a vast collection of Latin inscriptions. By turning each text into a kind of historical fingerprint, Aeneas identifies deep connections that can help historians situate inscriptions within their broader historical context.
F9.claim: parallels search across a vast collection of Latin inscriptions, each text a historical fingerprint
F9.lineage: parallels: what they are and how the model retrieves them

F10.locus: Aeneas’ advanced capabilities, Processing multimodal input; Restoring gaps
F10.quote: Aeneas is the first model to determine a text's geographical provenance using multimodal inputs. … For the first time, Aeneas can restore gaps in texts where the missing length is unknown.
F10.claim: the first model to determine geographical provenance from multimodal input, and to restore gaps of unknown length
F10.lineage: the tasks: multimodal provenance, restoration of unknown length, dating

F11.quote: drawing from decades of work by historians to create digital collections, especially the Epigraphic Database Roma (EDR), Epigraphic Database Heidelberg (EDH) and Epigraphic Database Clauss Slaby (EDCS-ELT). … We cleaned, harmonized and linked these records into a single machine-actionable dataset that we refer to as the Latin Epigraphic Dataset (LED), comprising over 176,000 Latin inscriptions from across the ancient Roman world.
F11.claim: the Latin Epigraphic Dataset: over 176,000 Latin inscriptions, cleaned, harmonized and linked from EDR, EDH and EDCS, the work of historians
F11.lineage: the corpus: the Latin Epigraphic Dataset

F12.quote: For each inscription, Aeneas’ contextualization mechanism retrieves a list of parallels using a technique called “embeddings” — encoding the textual and contextual information of each inscription into a kind of historical fingerprint
F12.claim: the contextualization mechanism retrieves parallels by embeddings, a historical fingerprint of each inscription
F12.lineage: parallels: what they are and how the model retrieves them

F13.quote: Aeneas restores damaged inscriptions with a Top-20 accuracy of 73% in gaps of up to ten characters. This only decreases to 58% when the restoration length is unknown … our model can attribute an inscription to one of 62 ancient Roman provinces with 72% accuracy. For dating, Aeneas places a text within 13 years of the date ranges provided by historians.
F13.claim: measured: top-20 restoration 73% (58% at unknown length); province among 62 at 72%; dating within 13 years of historians' ranges
F13.lineage: the tasks: multimodal provenance, restoration of unknown length, dating

F14.locus: A new lens on historical debates ¶2
F14.quote: Rather than predicting a single fixed date, Aeneas produced a detailed distribution of possible dates, showing two distinct peaks, with one smaller peak around 10-1  BCE and a larger, more confident peak between 10-20 CE. These results captured both prevailing dating hypotheses in a quantitative way.
F14.claim: on the Res Gestae the model gives a distribution of dates with two peaks, capturing both prevailing hypotheses
F14.lineage: the case studies: the Res Gestae and the Mainz altar

F15.quote: We invited twenty-three historians who regularly work with inscriptions to restore, date and place a set of texts using Aeneas. … the most effective results were achieved when historians used Aeneas’ contextual information alongside its predictions
F15.claim: a study with twenty-three historians; best results with the model's context and predictions together
F15.lineage: the historians' study and its figures

F16.locus: Sharing the tools, shaping the future ¶1
F16.quote: Aeneas is designed to integrate within historians' existing research workflows. By combining expert knowledge with machine learning, it opens up a collaborative process, offering interpretable suggestions that serve as valuable starting points for historical inquiry.
F16.claim: designed to integrate in historians' workflows, offering interpretable suggestions as starting points
F16.lineage: a tool in the historian's workflow

F17.locus: Sharing the tools, shaping the future ¶2
F17.quote: As part of today’s release, we’re upgrading Ithaca , our ancient Greek model, to be powered by Aeneas and include the contextualization function, restorations of unknown length and better performance overall.
F17.claim: Ithaca, the Greek model, is upgraded to be powered by Aeneas, with its contextualization function
F17.lineage: lineage and name: Ithaca, the hero

F18.quote: The research was co-led by Yannis Assael and Thea Sommerschield.
F18.claim: co-led by Yannis Assael and Thea Sommerschield
F18.lineage: who made it: DeepMind, the partners, the authors

F19.quote: While trained for Latin, Aeneas can be adapted to other ancient languages, scripts and media, from papyri to coinage.
F19.claim: trained for Latin; adaptable to other languages, scripts and media
F19.lineage: the stated reach: other languages, scripts and media

F20.quote: Aeneas can search for parallels (texts that share similarities in wording, syntax, standardized formulas or provenance) across thousands of Latin inscriptions, process multimodal input (text and images) and restore gaps in text, setting a new state-of-the-art benchmark in the field.
F20.claim: Google's blog restates the parallels search, multimodal input and gap restoration
F20.lineage: parallels: what they are and how the model retrieves them

F21.quote: A team of researchers, including Professor Jonathan Prag, an ancient historian in the Faculty of Classics, has just published a paper in Nature introducing Aeneas
F21.claim: Oxford's Faculty of Classics names Jonathan Prag among the paper's authors
F21.lineage: who made it: DeepMind, the partners, the authors

F22.quote: In a field of this sort, the answers are not black and white, and the data is simultaneously rich and incomplete. Aeneas takes a leap beyond Ithaca to provide humanities researchers with a level of support – based upon previous scholarship - that we could only previously have dreamed of.
F22.claim: Prag: answers in the field are not black and white, the data rich and incomplete; Aeneas a leap beyond Ithaca, its support based on previous scholarship
F22.lineage: a tool in the historian's workflow

F23.quote: Model: Aeneas is a generative neural network developed by Google DeepMind for contextualising ancient texts, performing arbitrary-length text restoration, visua...
F23.claim: the repository card: a generative neural network by Google DeepMind for contextualising ancient texts and arbitrary-length restoration
F23.lineage: access: the interface, the code, the dataset, the licence

F24.quote: However, current digital methods are restricted to literal matches and narrow historical scopes. Here we introduce Aeneas, a generative neural network for contextualizing ancient texts. Aeneas retrieves textual and contextual parallels, leverages visual inputs, handles arbitrary-length text restoration, and advances the state of the art in key tasks.
F24.claim: the paper's definition: a generative neural network for contextualizing ancient texts, against digital methods restricted to literal matches
F24.lineage: what it is: a model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions

F25.quote: Historians capture these insights by identifying parallels—inscriptions with shared phrasing, function or cultural setting—to enable the contextualization of texts within broader historical frameworks, and perform key tasks such as restoration and geographical or chronological attribution
F25.claim: the paper's definition of parallels: inscriptions with shared phrasing, function or cultural setting, used to contextualize, restore and attribute
F25.lineage: parallels: what they are and how the model retrieves them

F26.quote: The historians find the parallels retrieved by Aeneas to be useful research starting points in 90% of cases, improving their confidence in key tasks by 44%. Restoration and geographical attribution tasks yielded superior results when historians were paired with Aeneas, outperforming both humans and artificial intelligence alone. For dating, Aeneas achieved a 13-year distance from ground-truth ranges.
F26.claim: headline findings: parallels useful starting points in 90% of cases, confidence up 44%; historian with Aeneas beats either alone; dating at 13 years
F26.lineage: the historians' study and its figures

F27.quote: when provided with Aeneas’ parallels, historians reported that these could serve as a starting point for historical inquiry 75% of the time. This increased to 90% when Aeneas’ predictions for the three epigraphic tasks were also included. Moreover, Aeneas’ parallels boosted historians’ confidence by an average of 23%, with an additional 21% increase when Aeneas’ predictions were also available.
F27.claim: the figures' qualification: parallels alone 75% and +23% confidence; 90% and +44% (23 + 21) only with the model's predictions added
F27.lineage: the historians' study and its figures

F28.quote: encompassing inscriptions from the seventh century bce to the eighth century ce … The final LED comprises 176,861 inscriptions (totalling 16 million characters), most of which have damaged sections, and we were able to obtain corresponding images of 5% of inscriptions.
F28.claim: the LED: 176,861 inscriptions, seventh century BCE to eighth century CE, 16 million characters, images for 5%
F28.lineage: the corpus: the Latin Epigraphic Dataset

F29.quote: only the geographical attribution head incorporates the additional inputs from the vision network—the restoration and chronological attribution tasks do not use the visual modality.
F29.claim: images enter only geographical attribution; restoration and dating are text-only
F29.lineage: the tasks: multimodal provenance, restoration of unknown length, dating

F30.quote: Aeneas retrieves a list of the most relevant epigraphic parallels from the training set of LED. … This design enables the model to surpass traditional fuzzy string-matching methods, to include a wealth of epigraphic parallels from relevant places and periods, related concepts, synonymous terms, formulaic variations and analogous epigraphic practices.
F30.claim: parallels retrieved from the LED training set by historically enriched embeddings, beyond fuzzy string matching
F30.lineage: parallels: what they are and how the model retrieves them

F31.quote: This altar shares rare textual formulas and an identical iconographical type with Cogitatus’ dedication, supporting the hypothesis that the later inscription was directly influenced by the earlier one.
F31.claim: a retrieved parallel supports, by the authors' reading, the hypothesis that a later inscription was directly influenced by an earlier one
F31.lineage: the case studies: the Res Gestae and the Mainz altar

F32.quote: Aeneas’ chronological attribution of the full text of the RGDA reflects prevailing scholarly hypotheses, with a distribution exhibiting a strong bimodal pattern
F32.claim: the RGDA dating reflects prevailing hypotheses in a bimodal distribution
F32.lineage: the case studies: the Res Gestae and the Mainz altar

F33.quote: Aeneas’ architecture outperforms the previous state-of-the-art model, offers multimodal capabilities, enables restoration of text sequences of unknown lengths, and can also be adapted to any ancient language and written medium (such as papyri, manuscripts or coinage).
F33.claim: the paper's statement of reach: adaptable to any ancient language and written medium, papyri and manuscripts among them
F33.lineage: the stated reach: other languages, scripts and media

F34.quote: the size of LED (16 million characters) remains a significant limitation compared with the scale of datasets typically used in state-of-the-art natural language processing research. … the available corpus is also subject to inherent biases, most significantly inscription survival bias, potentially skewing the data towards certain materials, locations, or historical contexts.
F34.claim: stated limits: the corpus is small for NLP and biased by inscription survival
F34.lineage: stated limits: data, bias, images, interpretation

F35.quote: performance often tends to be weaker where data is limited
F35.claim: performance weaker where data is limited, by decade and province
F35.lineage: stated limits: data, bias, images, interpretation

F36.quote: The Aeneas source code is available at https://github.com/google-deepmind/predictingthepast under Apache License 2.0, along with the trained weights, licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license (CC BY-SA 4.0).
F36.claim: code under Apache 2.0, weights under CC BY-SA 4.0, at the GitHub repository
F36.lineage: access: the interface, the code, the dataset, the licence

F37.quote: The name Aeneas is inspired by the wandering hero of Graeco-Roman mythology: like Aeneas, who journeyed from Troy across the Mediterranean seeking guidance on where to found the future city of Rome, our model seeks to uncover epigraphic parallels to ground historical research and link the past to the present.
F37.claim: the name: the wandering hero, as the model seeks parallels to ground research
F37.lineage: lineage and name: Ithaca, the hero

F38.quote: We therefore focus on Latin inscriptions, as this gap offers a valuable opportunity for interdisciplinary research with broader scholarly impact.
F38.claim: Latin chosen because few machine-learning studies treat Latin inscriptions
F38.lineage: the stated reach: other languages, scripts and media

F39.quote: To do this, Aeneas takes in partial transcriptions of an inscription alongside a scanned image of it. Using these, it gives possible dates and places of origins for the engraving, along with potential fill-ins for any missing text.
F39.claim: MIT Technology Review: from transcription and image the model gives possible dates, places and fill-ins
F39.lineage: the tasks: multimodal provenance, restoration of unknown length, dating

F40.quote: Aeneas also cross-references the text with a stored database of almost 150,000 inscriptions
F40.claim: MIT Technology Review's figure: a database of almost 150,000 inscriptions
F40.lineage: the corpus: the Latin Epigraphic Dataset

F41.quote: Rather than seeking to automate epigraphy—the research field dealing with deciphering and understanding inscriptions—he and his colleagues are interested in “crafting a tool that will integrate with the workflow of a historian,” Assael said in a press briefing.
F41.claim: Assael: not to automate epigraphy but a tool for the historian's workflow
F41.lineage: a tool in the historian's workflow

F42.quote: It doesn’t guess the meaning of texts, so it can’t interpret newly found engravings on its own, and it’s not clear yet how useful it will be to historians’ workflows in the long term, according to Kathleen Coleman, a professor of classics at Harvard. The Monumentum Ancyranum is considered to be one of the best-known and most well-studied inscriptions in epigraphy, raising the question of how Aeneas will fare on more obscure samples.
F42.claim: Coleman's limit: it does not guess meaning or interpret new finds alone, its long-term use unclear; the test case is among the best-studied inscriptions
F42.lineage: stated limits: data, bias, images, interpretation

F43.quote: showed that Aeneas helped spur research ideas among the historians for 90% of inscriptions
F43.claim: MIT Technology Review's restatement: research ideas for 90% of inscriptions
F43.lineage: the historians' study and its figures

F44.claim: the interface's own title: contextualising, restoring and attributing ancient texts
F44.lineage: access: the interface, the code, the dataset, the licence
